sn35.103:1.1: One of the Brahmanical sages under whom the Bodhisatta practiced before awakening ([mn26:16.1]()). Another of his enigmatic sayings is found at [dn29:16.8](). When the Bodhisatta began his study, he first learned to recite the scriptures, and in these two passages we find examples of what those scriptures were. While none of Uddaka’s teachings have been identified in the Vedic corpus, there is a short teaching passage in the Jain Isibhāsiyāiṁ, which collects sayings of various sages, including Buddhists and Vedists. Chapter 23 is attributed to a certain Rāmaputta, who is likely the same person. The identification is supported by the Pali text here.
sn35.103:1.2: The idiom of this verse is very unlike the suttas. There seems no reason to doubt it is a genuine quote, but I have not been able to trace it as such. | The initial pronoun _idaṁ_ is neuter, and serves as an emphatic particle disconnected from the masculine nouns. Compare the use of _idam_ at Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa 3.6.1.5, 3.7.1.2, 13.8.2.15. | A similar phrasing is employed by Brahmā Sahampati at [sn6.13:5.1](), where it emphasizes direct experience. | In early Sanskrit and Pali, _jātu_ usually has the sense “ever” or the emphatic “absolutely” (here, commentary glosses _ekaṁsena_; see too Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa 2.2.2.20, 14.6.8.1). | _Vedagū_ is not attested in Brahmanical texts, but it is perhaps a contraction of Sanskrit _vedapāraga_ in the same sense: “one versed in the Vedas”, such as Yājñavalkya (Mahābhārata 1.113.40). Given that in Buddhist literature it is assumed to be a term of the brahmins, perhaps the Buddha learned it under Uddaka from this very line.
sn35.103:1.4: The terms “dug” (_palikhata_ = Ardhamāgadhī _paḍighāta_) and “boil” (_gaṇḍa_), neither of which are particularly common, occur multiple times in Isibhāsiyāiṁ 23. It is remarkable that, although so few of Uddaka’s teachings are preserved, they contain this striking language in common. It attests to a common source in the Buddhist and Jain texts. Probably these were terms used by Uddaka himself. Perhaps “boil”, like “knowledge master” was adapted by the Buddha from this passage.
sn35.103:1.6: The story of the Bodhisatta’s studentship under Uddaka implies that he had not attained the highest meditation that he taught ([mn26:16.9](), etc.). Nonetheless, the Buddha respected him, which suggests that in making these claims he was not knowingly lying. He likely believed that he had attained, but his understanding was insufficient by the Buddha’s standards.
sn35.103:4.2: Also at [an9.15:2.1](). Elsewhere, “boil” is a term for sensual pleasures ([an6.23]()) or for suffering ([sn22.122:1.4]()).
